latency_note: total_latency_ms = ttft_ms + tpot_ms * output_tokens, normalised to 32 output tokens for every engine so the comparison is like for like. Fennec's ttft_ms and tpot_ms are measured directly: the prompt is walked one position at a time, the step at index prompt_len-1 emits the first output token, TTFT is the sum up to and including it, and TPOT is the mean of the steps after it. Fennec's own wall_ms equals its total_latency_ms because it generated exactly 32 tokens. For the other engines tpot_ms is derived, not instrumented, and the basis is recorded per row: where a run reports both a completion-token count and a TTFT, TPOT is (tokens/tok_s - ttft)/(tokens-1); where it does not, TPOT falls back to 1000/tok_s, which amortises prefill across every token and therefore overstates the true decode-only cost. Derived values are marked and should be read as approximate.

fennec_variants_note: The int4 container is the checkpoint the suite ships. Both GPU rows are the shipped default on one build: same 8 threads, same 7.77 GiB budget read off the card, same 2304 device experts and the same 30.1% device hit rate, so the pick split is identical and the difference is the device tier alone. CUDA wins end to end — 77.5 vs 84.2 ms of stack and 7.9 vs 10.1 ms of lm_head, 11.71 vs 10.61 tok/s. The head gap is the readback, not the kernel: on the same f16 head CUDA measures 4.8 ms compute + 0.33 ms readback against Vulkan's 5.0 + 2.25, because Vulkan's host-visible coherent arena reads back through an uncached mapping. CUDA also loads faster (11.4-11.9 s against 14.5-15.4 s) because its device upload is 5.5-5.8 s against Vulkan's 8.6-8.7 s. The bf16 row is historical and was measured on the retracted decode basis; it is not comparable and has not been re-run.

fennec_kernel_fix.what: The AVX2 int4 dot kernel was gated on group == 32. The shipped int4 container uses group 64, so every host expert fell back to the scalar nibble loop.
fennec_kernel_fix.note: Same checkpoint, same machine, same 8 threads. Only the CPU kernel changed: 2.50x on CPU+GPU, 1.60x on CPU alone. The group-32 path is bit-identical, so the bf16 row did not move.

fennec_cuda_fix.what: The CUDA activation arena was pinned host memory (cuMemHostAlloc), so every kernel read its activations over PCIe. That is a Vulkan idiom: Vulkan's host-visible coherent arena is cheap, CUDA's zero-copy memory is not. Switching to a device-local cuMemAlloc arena with explicit HtoD/DtoH in write/read, plus ld.global.nc on the read-only weight and scale loads, fixed it.
fennec_cuda_fix.note: A balanced-tree dot product was also tried and measured worse (142 GB/s against 152 for the dependent FMA chain), so it was reverted: the gemv is memory-bound, not latency-bound. All 7 GPU integration tests pass through FENNEC_BACKEND=cuda at ~1e-7 relative RMS.

fennec_vram_finding.what: The default --device budget was a flat 8.0 GiB, which on an 8 GiB card commits right up to the physical limit. WDDM then places the allocation that exceeds the process budget in system memory, and the loser is whichever buffer went up last: the lm_head. It is the worst possible loser — 0.95 GiB read once per token, against roughly 224 MiB of expert picks — so every token paid a PCIe round trip for a buffer the kernels believed was local.
fennec_vram_finding.how_it_was_found: The isolated lm_head test measures 4.8 ms compute + 0.33 ms readback on CUDA and 5.0 + 2.25 on Vulkan, yet decode reported 45.9 ms and 15.7 ms for the same call. The kernel and the transfer were both ruled out by timing them separately (tests/gpu.rs now prints both legs). The only remaining difference was the 7.6 GiB expert pool resident alongside the head, so the budget was swept.
fennec_vram_finding.conclusion: The cliff is real but it is not backend-neutral. CUDA's head collapses from 45.9 ms to 5.1 ms as soon as the budget leaves headroom, and 7.0 GiB is the best budget-only result (9.04 tok/s against 7.17). Vulkan tolerates a near-full card far better — its head only falls 15.7 to 11.2 ms — so cutting its budget to 7.0 GiB trades 11 points of device hit rate for 4 ms and comes out behind (7.14 against 7.99). A single blanket headroom fraction would therefore regress the Vulkan tier.
fennec_vram_finding.fix: Two changes, and the second matters more than the first. (1) load_plan uploads the lm_head before the expert pool, so when WDDM demotes the allocation that exceeds the process budget it demotes an expert buffer (~1.7 MiB) instead of the 0.95 GiB head. (2) The default --device budget is read off the card (7.77 GiB usable) rather than assumed to be 8.0 GiB, so nothing is over-committed in the first place. A 0.875 headroom fraction was implemented first, measured, and reverted: it cut the budget too far and regressed Vulkan. Reading the real size is not the same as guessing a fraction of it.

fennec_vram_finding.decomposition_reading: Over-committing the card is bad on both backends; head-first only changes which buffer pays for it. At a true 8.0 GiB the head goes from 45.9 to 6.5 ms on CUDA, but the stack rises 93.6 to 117.3 ms because the demoted buffers are now experts and every pick of a demoted expert crosses PCIe. Net 139.5 to 123.8 ms, 1.13x. Dropping the budget to the card's real 7.77 GiB removes the demotion entirely: 140 fewer resident experts (2.1 points of hit rate) buy back 25.8 ms of stack, 123.8 to 98.0 ms, another 1.26x. Combined 1.42x on CUDA. On Vulkan head-first alone is neutral-to-slightly-negative (7.99 to 7.74, inside the spread) and essentially the whole 1.06x comes from not over-committing. So the card-derived budget is the load-bearing fix and head-first is insurance for when the budget is still too large — another process holding VRAM, or a card whose usable size is reported optimistically.
fennec_vram_finding.fix_tradeoff: The shipped default holds 2304 experts in VRAM against 2444 at a flat 8.0 GiB, and the measured device hit rate is 39.3% against 41.4%. Those 140 experts are not worth anything if their buffers are demoted to system memory: giving them up removes the demotion and is worth 25.8 ms/token on CUDA. The planner's predicted device hit rate is still optimistic, since its head reservation does not fully bound what the runtime can upload, and it predicted 51.8% where the runtime achieved 39.3%. Recorded as an open accounting defect, not silently corrected.

variance_note: Run-to-run variance on this laptop is large and any single number misleads. On the CURRENT build, with routing proven identical (dev_hits 3855 in every run), five CUDA runs measured 10.79, 11.45, 11.71, 11.85 and 12.16 tok/s and three Vulkan runs 10.54, 10.61 and 11.23 — a 13% spread on CUDA and 6% on Vulkan, from machine noise alone. Earlier revisions of this note quoted 4.88-8.47 tok/s for Vulkan; that spread was across BUILDS and across the retracted decode basis, and is kept in fennec_vram_finding as history. fennec_cli_fix.what: Opts::has() inspected only the valueless-flag list, never the key/value map. The parser puts `--gpu` in flags but `--device 8` in kv, so has("device") was false for every spelling of a valued option. setup() gated the GPU budget on has("device"), which meant --device was silently dropped and every run used the card-derived default.
fennec_cli_fix.how_it_was_found: `plan --device 8.0 --json` reported device_gib 7.76953125 — the card's usable size, not 8.0. Two runs that should have differed by 0.23 GiB produced byte-identical plans.
fennec_cli_fix.blast_radius: Only --device was gated on has() with a value; the other has() callers (json, cpu, curve, verbose, allow-remote, no-think, greedy, auto-tier) are valueless flags and behaved correctly. gpu_wanted() already checked both maps explicitly, which is why --gpu 1 worked. No suite benchmark script passes --device, so no archived result was invalidated. The manual VRAM sweep predates the gate and called opts.num("device") directly, so it is valid; the two head-first rows that postdate the gate are relabelled 6.8 GiB in fennec_vram_finding.fix_measured_caveat.
fennec_cli_fix.fix: has() now returns true if the key is in either map, and gpu_wanted()'s redundant kv check was removed. Two parser regression tests cover both spellings, the indexed --gpu form, and --cpu overriding it.

cuda_competitors.question: Can Colibri, rabbit or fox be measured on the CUDA tier on this machine?
cuda_competitors.answer: No. None of the three can run CUDA here, for three different reasons. Fennec is the only engine in this comparison with a working CUDA tier on this box.

rabbit.evidence: Cargo.toml has no [features] section at all (49 lines). src/expert_cache.rs:41 states 'any VRAM/CUDA promotion (no CUDA backend here)'. Kernels are x86 SIMD only (src/kernels.rs:92-96, AVX2/AVX-512/VNNI tiers). The only tuning flag is --threads (src/main.rs:99). io-uring is Linux-only (Cargo.toml:33-34).
rabbit.consequence: rabbit's 0.71 tok/s is a CPU-only number and is the only number it can produce.

fox.verdict: not buildable here - CUDA is gated on a toolkit that is absent
fox.evidence: build.rs:316 enables GGML_CUDA only if CUDACXX or `which nvcc` resolves; vendor/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/CMakeLists.txt:3 find_package(CUDAToolkit), :59 enable_language(CUDA), :37 89-real for Ada. Probes: `where nvcc` absent, `where cl` absent, the default CUDA toolkit install directory absent, both Visual Studio directories absent. cmake is present (WinLibs MinGW) but MinGW gcc is not a valid nvcc host compiler. No ggml-cuda.dll exists anywhere in the suite; the prebuilt set in target/release/build/ferrumox-*/out/bin is ggml-vulkan.dll, ggml-cpu.dll, ggml-base.dll, ggml.dll, libllama.dll, libllama-common.dll, libmtmd.dll. the system copy of nvcuda.dll is present, so the driver is there - only the compiler is missing.
fox.no_igpu_mismeasurement: fox's published 12.00 tok/s was already on the discrete card: bench_fox_vulkan2.log:61 reads 'using device Vulkan1 (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 Laptop GPU) - 7188 MiB free'. Device 0 is the Intel Arc iGPU (uma:1), device 1 the RTX 4060 (uma:0, NV_coopmat2v). The number is honest.

colibri.verdict: CUDA exists in source but is not compiled into the shipped binary
colibri.evidence: The engine is pure C; Python is only a launcher/converter. c/backend_cuda.cu exists alongside backend_vulkan.c and backend_metal.mm, selected at runtime by COLI_CUDA=1 (c/qwen36_tier.c:871), devices by COLI_GPUS/COLI_GPU (:893-894), VRAM budget CUDA_EXPERT_GB (:706). But c/.build-config reads CUDA=0|CUDA_DLL=0|VK=1|XDNA=0 (gcc -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 -fopenmp -DCOLI_VULKAN), and a byte scan of c/qwen36.exe finds no coli_cuda.dll or coli_cuda_init strings.
colibri.consequence: The 20.06 tok/s baseline is CPU+Vulkan, not CUDA. It is the number to beat, and it was never a CUDA number.
colibri.what_a_cuda_run_would_need: make qwen36.exe CUDA_DLL=1 plus make cuda-dll (or c/build_cuda.bat, which auto-detects sm_89 for the 4060) to produce coli_cuda.dll beside the exe (c/Makefile:1397-1409,1020-1032). Linux links CUDA=1 directly; Windows refuses it (Makefile:596-597). Both need nvcc and an MSVC host compiler, neither of which is on this box.
colibri.torch_is_irrelevant: torch 2.15.0+cpu is installed (cuda available False) but appears only in c/tools/convert_*.py, never in inference. There is no torch fallback that would silently use CUDA.

cuda_competitors.fennec_cuda: Fennec's CUDA tier needs no toolkit and no MSVC: it goes through the Driver API with hand-written PTX compiled at runtime by cuModuleLoadDataEx. All 9 GPU integration tests pass on the RTX 4060 at ~1e-7 relative RMS under FENNEC_BACKEND=cuda, including one that moves the device handle to another thread — the pattern `serve` uses and the one that exposed the per-thread context bug.

colibri_host_expert_mechanism.why_it_matters: Colibri's 43.18 ms TPOT against Fennec's 82.37 ms is not mostly a memory-placement difference. Four mechanisms were read out of the source.
colibri_host_expert_mechanism.kernel: Native C + OpenMP + AVX2. int4 nibbles are dotted directly, never dequantised to f32. Activations are quantised to int8 once per row and the dot is vpdpbusd: xf_dot_i8_avx2, c/expert_ffn.h:254-269. Unsigned nibble x int8 activation, with the -8 weight bias removed as one per-group correction. Experts stay planar int4 in RAM (c/qwen36.c:1666-1701, default on for gs=64 containers; QWEN_EXPERT_KERNEL=0 restores the unpack-to-int8 path).
colibri_host_expert_mechanism.kernel_claimed_gain: c/qwen36.c:1677-1680 records 'activations to int8 once per row, dpbusd against the planar nibbles. Measured on the 35B: expert compute 22.7 to 15.9 ms/token for +0.1% perplexity.' That is the whole expert stack, against Fennec's 36.63 ms for host picks alone.
colibri_host_expert_mechanism.work_queue: All top-8 picks are batched into one (expert, row-chunk) queue, deduped by expert and chunked to 4*T items so every thread works (c/expert_ffn.h:820-898 xf_moe_compute; r16 variant 706-813).
colibri_host_expert_mechanism.thread_sizing: Threads = physical cores, not logical (coli_omp_tune_threads, c/qwen36.c:9351; c/omp_tune.h:102-114). The comment at c/qwen36.c:9344-9348 records +2.3x from sizing alone on a 16C/32T part.
colibri_host_expert_mechanism.zero_copy_host_pool: Every expert lives in a HOST_VISIBLE|HOST_COHERENT Vulkan buffer in system RAM that the device reads directly (host_init, c/vk_tier.c:2653-2707; COLI_VK_TIER_HOST_GB, promote rate COLI_VK_TIER_PROMOTE=32). With COLI_VK_HYBRID the CPU computes some resident pairs in place in that same mapped buffer while the GPU runs its batch (host_pairs, c/vk_tier.c:2051-2128, join at 2400-2410) - no RAM copy, no disk.
colibri_host_expert_mechanism.hit_rate_is_understated: The reported device percentage is T.served/T.routed over routed picks (vkt_report, c/vk_tier.c:3118-3133). Hybrid pairs computed in place by the CPU are marked taken but not counted in T.served (:2368 precedes :2372), so 58.5% device understates GPU-pool coverage and the CPU remainder is far below 166 full-cost picks.
colibri_host_expert_mechanism.cold_load: No mmap: pread + O_DIRECT + fadvise(DONTNEED) (c/st.h:3-5). Startup loads the int8-quantised dense trunk (COLI_DENSE_BITS=8 default, c/qwen36.c:1799) plus only the planner's VRAM set, in a parallel OpenMP warmstart (:9326-9337). Every other expert is lazy: first routed touch reads from disk into an LRU RAM cache (expert_fetch, :4651-4707) with a PILOT prefetch thread 1-3 layers ahead (:6521-6534,7041). TTFT is fast because prefill streams cold experts through device slots and computes them on the GPU (c/vk_tier.c:1003,1278 issue_big; loader callback vk_load, c/qwen36.c:9214).
colibri_host_expert_mechanism.no_skipped_experts: Every pick is computed - device, hybrid in place, or CPU fallback. Failed batches are recomputed (c/vk_tier.c:2433-2445).

comparison_asymmetries.why: The 20.06 tok/s baseline is not a like-for-like configuration against Fennec's rows. Three differences are disclosed rather than hidden, and none of them is an excuse: Fennec is still behind.
comparison_asymmetries.threads: Colibri ran 16 threads; Fennec ran 8, a courtesy cap so the machine stayed usable during measurement. Colibri sizes its pool to physical cores (coli_omp_tune_threads) and records +2.3x from sizing alone on a 16C/32T part. This host is a hybrid Core Ultra 7 155H: 6 P-cores (logical 0-11), 8 E-cores (12-19), 2 LP-E (20-21). Fennec has NO thread affinity anywhere - bare std::thread::spawn, and set_threads only sizes the pool - so its 8 workers can land on E-cores. That is a suspected part of the host-expert gap and is unmeasured.
comparison_asymmetries.host_tier: Colibri ran with COLI_VK_TIER_HOST_GB=4, a 4 GiB host tier, against Fennec's 13.08 GiB. A smaller host tier means more of Colibri's picks are served from the device or computed in place in a mapped buffer, which is cheaper than Fennec's DRAM-resident f32 dot.
comparison_asymmetries.backend: Colibri's 20.06 is CPU+Vulkan, not CUDA: c/.build-config reads CUDA=0|CUDA_DLL=0|VK=1|XDNA=0. Fennec's best row is CUDA. The comparison is therefore Vulkan-C against Rust-CUDA, which favours Fennec on the device tier and still loses.
comparison_asymmetries.hit_rate_basis: Colibri's 58.5% is T.served/T.routed over routed picks and excludes hybrid pairs the CPU computed in place in the mapped buffer, so it understates GPU-pool coverage. Fennec's 30.1% counts every device-served pick. The two percentages are not the same statistic.

fennec_decode_fidelity.what: RETRACTION. The decode benchmark's loop pushed its argmax on every iteration, including the prompt phase. At t == prompt_len it therefore read toks[prompt_len] = the prediction from position 0, not from the whole prompt, so the timed continuation was not the greedy sequence `serve` produces. Every Fennec throughput number published before this fix was measured on a wrong token sequence.
fennec_decode_fidelity.fix: main.rs now pushes only when t + 1 >= prompt_len, matching serve.rs's existing `if t + 1 < ids.len() { continue; }` guard.
fennec_decode_fidelity.how_it_was_found: After the fix the CUDA TPOT rose 69.31 -> 90.998 ms, which looked like a 31% regression. It was not noise: dev_hits fell 5030 -> 3855 (39.3% -> 30.1%) while placement was byte-identical (2304 device experts, 7936 host, 10240 resident, 13.078125 GiB FQ4, group 64). The device-hit counter is a pure function of routing, so the sequence had changed. `moe host experts` rose 30.40 -> 44.70 ms/token, which is the whole difference.

fennec_fused_mixer.what: The gated delta net's conv and recurrence used to run on the CPU, forcing a device round trip across all 30 linear-attention layers. Both are now device kernels (gdn_conv, gdn_rec) and the whole linear-attention block is one batch: write x, four gemv_half projections, gdn_conv, gdn_rec, gemv_half out_proj, run, read. One h-float write and one h-float read per layer instead of five round trips.
fennec_fused_mixer.kernels: gdn_conv: 256 threads, cd/256 groups, bindings [scratch, conv_w, conv_state, dummy]. gdn_rec: 512 threads, nv groups, bindings [scratch, params, rec_state, dummy], push exactly 8 u32. Shared layout sq[256]@0 sk[256]@1024 so[256]@2048 tmp[512]@3072 = 5120 bytes; G = 512/dv, rows = dk/G. This model has dk = dv = 128, so G = 4 and rows = 32.
fennec_fused_mixer.shape_guard: Falls back to the split path when dk or dv is 0 or > 256, nv is 0, nk is 0, nv % nk != 0, 512 % dv != 0, rows == 0, dk % (512/dv) != 0 or rows % 4 != 0. No silent CPU fallback for a shape the kernel can handle.
fennec_fused_mixer.state_ownership: GdnState.mirrored tracks whether the device holds the current conv/rec state. The fused path uploads on first use and sets it; sync_state reads back and clears it. Chosen over pointer identity because serve.rs calls model.states() per request and a freed Vec's address can be reused. Safe because serve.rs holds the model mutex for the whole generation loop.
fennec_fused_mixer.measured: fused_mixer_matches_the_cpu_mixer_and_its_state passes at ~2.7e-7 relative RMS against a 2e-5 band, on both backends.
fennec_fused_mixer.profiler_caveat: Stage names are NOT comparable across this change. In the old split path the MIXER_CPU timer was started before the second device match, so out_proj and its fence counted as mixer host. After fusion, `mixer host` is the 10 full-attention layers only. Only totals and TPOT are comparable.

fennec_pinned_arena_reverted.what: NULL RESULT, reverted. An audit read cudagpu.rs's module doc — which claimed a cuMemHostAlloc arena with plain-memcpy accessors — concluded the synchronous HtoD/DtoH copies were a bug, and supplied a patch to make the arena pinned and device-mapped. The doc was stale; the code was already device-local, deliberately.
fennec_pinned_arena_reverted.why: CUDA zero-copy is a Vulkan idiom that does not transfer. The gemv re-reads the same x once per row, so a mapped arena puts every one of those reads on PCIe. The lm_head regression 5.0 -> 8.3 ms is the canary, and it is the same direction fennec_cuda_fix already recorded from a prior session (6.7 ms pinned against 4.7 device-local).
fennec_pinned_arena_reverted.action: cuda.rs reverted to net zero change; cudagpu.rs's arena code restored to cuMemAlloc + explicit write/read. The real defect was the doc, which is rewritten to state device-local and cite the measurement. Kept from the episode: a cols % group guard in upload_q4 on both backends.

fennec_correctness_fixes.what: Ten correctness defects found by a read-only audit and fixed, each verified on both backends. Two were critical.
critical: serve.rs: a prompt at or past max_ctx panicked mid-forward inside the model mutex, poisoning it for every later request. Now refused with an error, and max_new is clamped to what fits (returning finish_reason 'length' when nothing fits).

serve.rs: streaming decoded one token at a time with a lossy UTF-8 conversion, so a multi-byte character split across two tokens became a permanent U+FFFD. Now the raw bytes are accumulated and only the valid prefix is emitted (Tokenizer::decode_bytes).
others: main.rs: the decode-fidelity bug — see fennec_decode_fidelity.
main.rs: printed 'CUDA and Metal are not implemented' whenever COLI_CUDA or COLI_METAL was set, which is false on both counts. Deleted.
main.rs: a .coli_usage histogram for a different model was accepted and would silently drop layers or index past the expert table. Now refused unless layers and experts both match the config.
safetensors.rs: DType::F64 did `raw as f64 as f32`, numeric-casting the bit pattern instead of reinterpreting it. Now f64::from_bits(raw) as f32.
safetensors.rs: slice_f32 accepted a backwards range. Now an error.
sched.rs: the scale-byte estimate used floor division where Q4::ngroups uses div_ceil, underestimating scales for a short final group. No effect on this model (2048/64 and 512/64 are exact).
model.rs: the fused path's `normed` offset is now rounded to 16 bytes, because CUDA's half gemv reads x as v4.f32. A no-op at nv = 32, a real fix for an odd nv.
gpu.rs / cudagpu.rs: upload_q4 now refuses cols % group != 0 rather than letting the shader read the next row's scale.
fennec_correctness_fixes.regression_test: tests/tokenizer.rs streaming_a_token_at_a_time_keeps_split_characters_intact asserts the naive per-token decode really did produce U+FFFD, so it proves the bug rather than only exercising the fix. It is the 76th test.

The first device call on a request thread died with 'CUDA write_buf 239: cuMemcpyHtoD: invalid device context' at model.rs:997, and the client saw ConnectionResetError WinError 10054.

blockers.tensorrt_not_available: Neither classic TensorRT nor TensorRT RTX is installed. A name search for tensorrt|nvinfer|nvonnxparser across Program Files, Program Files (x86), the whole DriverStore FileRepository, ProgramData and D: returned only the two files this investigation had just downloaded itself. The NVIDIA installs present are NVIDIA App, NvTelemetry and PhysX — no TensorRT package and no NVIDIA GPU Computing Toolkit directory. See ort_nvrtx_verdict for the TensorRT RTX specifics.
blockers.cuda_ep_runtime_absent: RETRACTED 2026-11-13: the runtime is NOT absent. The earlier claim quoted the ort crate's 'CUDA >= 13.2 / cuDNN >= 9.23' wording, which matches nothing official — ORT 1.27+ PyPI GPU packages are built against CUDA 13.0 and need CUDA 13.0+ / cuDNN 9.x. We installed onnxruntime-gpu 1.32.0 plus the NVIDIA CUDA 13 / cuDNN 9 redistributable wheels into a local directory (no system install, no permanent PATH change) and MEASURED the CUDA EP under Smart App Control: providers Tensorrt+CUDA+CPU, every capi DLL and .pyd Authenticode Valid, lm_head f16 4.983 ms vs Fennec's CUDA 5.24 ms (level). See benchmarks/results-ort-gpu-lane.json. What remains true: no nvcc/cl/CUDA Toolkit on PATH, only the driver's nvcuda.dll — which is why Fennec uses the Driver API with hand-written PTX and no ~2 GB runtime. The CPU EP wheel (1.31.1) registers only Azure+CPU and has no F16 MatMul kernel; it folds the F16 weights to F32.
blockers.no_onnx_model: Zero .onnx files under the model root. The shipped checkpoint is 43 int4-packed safetensors shards: a 256-expert MoE with a custom gated-delta-net linear-attention block that no stock exporter handles. The only non-safetensors model present is an OpenVINO IR embedder (bge-base-en-v1.5-int8-ov, .xml/.bin).
blockers.npu_blocked_below_ort: SCOPE CORRECTED 2026-11-12: the refusal covers DirectML only, not every ORT EP. Live probe: Intel(R) AI Boost, graphics=false generic_ml=true, D3D12CreateDevice refused 0x887a0004 DXGI_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED. ORT's DirectML EP creates a D3D12 device, so it sits above that refusal and cannot reach the NPU. ORT's OpenVINO EP does NOT go through D3D12 and is not covered by this blocker — see openvino_npu_measured and ort_openvino_verdict. The earlier wording 'no ONNX Runtime execution provider can reach it either' was wrong and is retracted.
blockers.no_tiered_residency: ORT owns its session allocator. It cannot express 2304 experts in VRAM / 8945 in RAM / cold experts streamed from NVMe, which is the whole design. Same reason TensorRT was rejected earlier.
blockers.offline_build: ort is absent from Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock and the offline registry cache; there is no vendor/ and no .cargo/config.toml. download-binaries and copy-dylibs are DEFAULT features, so adding ort fetches from pyke's CDN at build time and breaks the documented cargo build --release --offline. crates.io is reachable (HTTP 200), so a fetch is possible but changes the build contract.

On this box every GPU EP would fail to register, so an ort wrapper without .error_on_failure() would silently run CPU-only at 3.00 tok/s while appearing to work. nvidia_is_a_kernel_selection_fallback_no.evidence: Per-node exec_type profiling of the same graph on both GPUs. The same 72 FullyConnectedCompressed MatMul nodes run 'fully_connected_gpu_bf_tiled__f16' on GPU.0 for 8.44 ms total, but 'fully_connected_gpu_bfyx_ref__f32' on GPU.1 for 233.78 ms total — 27.7x. backend_matrix.why_a_new_protocol: The published table compared Fennec's instrumented decode loop against Colibri's HTTP server, so the two columns were not the same measurement. This matrix runs every engine through its own server and one streaming /v1/chat/completions request, at the same context, the same token budget and the same greedy sampler, median of 3 after two discarded full-length warm-ups.

backend_matrix.token_count_source: usage.completion_tokens from the final SSE chunk, not a count of SSE frames. A frame can carry a partial character or several tokens, and a reasoning model can spend the whole budget in reasoning_content while content stays empty. The harness raises if usage reports zero.
backend_matrix.prompt_cache_defeat: Every visit sends a different prompt prefix (`[probe 003] ...`), issued from a counter that belongs to the server process being measured. llama.cpp 1.0 selects a slot by longest-common-prefix similarity and keeps the matching KV - its own log said `selected slot by LCP similarity, f_sim_best = 1.000, f_keep = 0.300` and then priced the request at `prompt eval time = 202.03 ms / 4 tokens` where the same 27-token prompt uncached cost 1893.83 ms. Fennec and Colibri recompute the whole prompt every time, so an identical prompt every visit compared a cached prefill against an uncached one and made the gap look 10x. A suffix nonce would not fix it: LCP reuse skips the tail. The tag is the same per visit index in every cell, so paired and ABBA lanes still see identical work.

sentences: The fennec fox has unusually large ears for its body size.

npu_rust_lane.fidelity_note: Cosine against the CPU lane on real tokenized text, both flattened over the whole [1,128,768] output and mask-weighted mean-pooled to a 768-vector. An earlier 0.83 cosine came from feeding random token ids to an int8-calibrated model and is withdrawn.
npu_rust_lane.cpu_threads_note: The CPU lane is capped at 8 threads so this benchmark does not saturate the machine. The Python reference used OpenVINO's default thread count, so the two CPU figures are not directly comparable; NPU and GPU are unaffected by this setting.
npu_rust_lane.cpu_variance_disclosure: The CPU lane is the only unstable cell: per-run medians of 38.72 ms and 45.65 ms were observed in separate invocations. The Windows Defender process (MsMpEng) was measured at 63-69% CPU during one of them. NPU, Arc and RTX 4060 were unaffected: their per-repeat medians agree to within 0.3%, 3.5% and 0.05% respectively.
npu_rust_lane.hetero_disclosure: MULTI:NPU,CPU reports EXECUTION_DEVICES 'NPU.3720 CPU', so both devices genuinely participate. HETERO:NPU,CPU reports 'NPU' alone: the whole graph fit on the NPU, so the CPU half was not used in this run. Neither is a throughput win over the NPU by itself at this batch size.
npu_rust_lane.rtx4060_anomaly_reproduced_from_rust: GPU.1 is 236 ms against the Arc's 10.2 ms and the NPU's 12.2 ms. DEVICE_ARCHITECTURE reads 'GPU: vendor=0x10de arch=v8.9.0' for the NVIDIA card - the CUDA compute capability misread as an Intel uArch - against 'arch=v12.71.4' for the Arc. The kernel selector therefore matches nothing and falls back to the scalar reference OpenCL kernels. This reproduces the Python finding from Rust; it is not noise.

two_loader_bugs_found_and_fixed: openvino-sys forwards the path straight to libloading::Library::new, which on Windows is LoadLibraryExW(path, 0, 0). Handing it the libs directory fails; it needs the openvino_c.dll file itself.

With flags 0 the dependency search starts at the executable's directory, so openvino.dll sitting beside openvino_c.dll is not found. Prepending the runtime directory to the process PATH puts it in the standard search order.
npu_rust_lane.harness_bug_found_and_fixed: The first version split the device list on ',', which cut MULTI:NPU,CPU into MULTI:NPU and ran the NPU alone while labelling it heterogeneous. The separator is now ';'. The truncated cells were discarded and re-measured, not published.
npu_rust_lane.not_yet_wired_into_fennec: This is a standalone lane crate, deliberately outside the engine repo so the engine's offline build does not acquire the dependency. Wiring it behind an optional feature is a separate decision; nothing in the engine changed.

burn_cubecl_lane.request: unblock what is possible: vendor Burn + CubeCL and measure the MoE kernels in Rust
burn_cubecl_lane.status: CPU MEASURED, VULKAN BLOCKED UPSTREAM - a full-model lane is still impossible on this box
burn_cubecl_lane.scope: KERNEL-LEVEL, not full model. The dominant decode kernels at the checkpoint's exact shapes, on Burn's Flex and CubeCL backends.
burn_cubecl_lane.what_changed: Two earlier claims are withdrawn. (1) 'Neither burn nor cubecl is in the offline registry cache, so adding them breaks cargo build --offline' was wrong: cargo fetch pulled 357 crates into the shared cache and 689 packages locked, and the offline build resolves them with no vendoring. The lane is a standalone crate outside the engine, so Fennec's own dependency list is untouched. (2) 'Burn has no int4' was too coarse: 4-bit block storage exists, fused 4-bit compute does not. What did NOT get unblocked: every CubeCL/Vulkan cell panics inside cubecl-ir before a kernel runs, so the only measured cells are Burn's pure-Rust Flex CPU backend.
burn_cubecl_lane.api_note: Burn 0.22 erased the backend type parameter: Tensor<D, K> carries no B, and the device a tensor was created on selects the runtime. One code path runs on CPU and on both Vulkan adapters unchanged. Backend types still exist (burn_flex::Flex, burn_wgpu::Wgpu = Fusion<CubeBackend>) but are not needed to write a kernel.
burn_cubecl_lane.protocol: 10 warm-ups then 30 timed iterations per repeat, median of 3 repeats, weights regenerated per repeat. Each iteration ends in a one-scalar readback because CubeCL queues asynchronously and burn-fusion defers execution; the readback is the sync point. Flex's rayon pool is capped via RAYON_NUM_THREADS before the first tensor.
burn_cubecl_lane.cpu_threads_note: RAYON_NUM_THREADS is set before the first tensor, so Flex's rayon pool is capped at this count. 8 matches every Fennec figure in this suite.
burn_cubecl_lane.timing_method: each iteration ends in a one-scalar readback, because CubeCL queues asynchronously and burn-fusion defers execution; the readback is the sync point. Weights are regenerated per repeat, so a repeat is not just re-reading a warm cache.

projected_ms_per_token.note: Burn's projection is per-kernel x 40 layers, the same workload Fennec's stage profile reports. It is NOT a token rate: no attention, no sampling, no KV, no residency traffic. Comparing it to a full decode tok/s would be meaningless.

burn_cubecl_lane.precision_caveat: Burn 0.22.1 has quantize/quantize_dynamic/dequantize and a 4-bit block dtype (mxfp4 per_block[32] UE8M0, nvfp4 per_block[16] UE4M3), but NO fused quantized matmul anywhere in burn-tensor, burn-backend, burn-cubecl or cubecl. These GEMMs therefore run on dequantized f32 weights, reading 8x the bytes Fennec's int4 group-64 kernel reads with the dequant fused into the dot. Not a like-for-like kernel comparison.

cubecl_cpu_not_measured.chain: burn/cpu -> burn-cpu -> cubecl/cpu -> cubecl-cpu -> cubecl-llvm -> tracel-llvm-bundler
cubecl_cpu_not_measured.consequence: the CPU cell here is Burn's Flex backend, not CubeCL-on-CPU. Flex is the backend Burn 0.22 itself recommends (NdArray and LibTorch are deprecated in favour of it), and it is pure Rust, so it also satisfies the no-C/C++ constraint. The GPU cells are genuinely CubeCL.
cubecl_cpu_not_measured.detail: cubecl's CPU runtime JIT-compiles kernels through LLVM and links it statically. The bundler downloaded tracel-llvm-23.1.0-4-windows-x64.tar.xz (59,586,340 bytes) into the user cache but no extracted lib directory was produced, so the link line names archives that are not on disk. Clearing it needs a working LLVM install, which is a system-wide change this suite does not make.

cubecl_vulkan_blocked.status: BLOCKED - upstream panic, every one of the 6 Vulkan cells
cubecl_vulkan_blocked.panic_message: called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: "Expected type vector.vector <4 x cube.f32 > to implement dyn MaybeVectorizedType"
cubecl_vulkan_blocked.downstream_error: src/main.rs readback: "use `try_into_scalar` instead to catch the error at runtime: Execution(An error happened during execution Caused by: the work writing it was skipped 4 operation(s) below a failure)" - 3 operations for the router. The readback is reporting a kernel that never executed.
cubecl_vulkan_blocked.root_cause: Not a harness bug. cubecl-ir's vector_size() (interfaces/mod.rs:441-445) calls try_cast_ty!(ty, ctx, dyn MaybeVectorizedType) and unwraps it, while the sibling try_get_vector_size() (:447) uses the non-panicking type_cast::<dyn MaybeVectorizedType>(&*ty)?. The failing type is vector.vector, defined at types/mod.rs:29-46, and that definition DOES carry #[type_interface_impl] impl MaybeVectorizedType for VectorType returning self.vectorization. A second, unrelated VectorType (count/element_type) lives at types/spirv.rs:113-118 with its own impl. So the trait is implemented on the type that is being rejected: this is a pliron interface-registration failure inside cubecl-ir 0.11.4, upstream of anything this lane controls.

fusion_diagnostic.hypothesis: burn-fusion's deferred IR construction is what trips the cast
fusion_diagnostic.test: removed "fusion" from the lane's Cargo.toml features, rebuilt and reran all 9 cells
fusion_diagnostic.result: REFUTED - all 6 Vulkan cells panicked at the identical site with the identical message
fusion_diagnostic.consequence: fusion is not the cause. The canonical published run is the fusion-on one (results-burn-cubecl.json); the fusion-off run is kept only as the diagnostic that rules fusion out.

cubecl_vulkan_blocked.containment: Each cell runs inside catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(..)), so a panicking GPU cell is recorded with status/error and the CPU cells still publish. That is why this lane reports 3 measured cells and 6 blocked ones rather than nothing.
cubecl_vulkan_blocked.what_would_clear_it: A cubecl-ir release where the vector.vector type's MaybeVectorizedType interface is registered before vector_size() is called, or a Burn/CubeCL version pair that does not hit that path on Windows Vulkan. Neither is something this suite can patch without editing a vendored upstream crate.

why_not_full_model.verdict: Burn owns its allocator, so hot-in-VRAM / warm-in-RAM / cold-on-NVMe tiering is not expressible. Dequantized to the only precisions it can compute, the routed experts alone need 120 GiB at f32 or 60 GiB at f16 against 31.5 GiB of RAM and 8 GiB of VRAM. A full-model Burn lane cannot run on this box.

burn_cubecl_lane.colibri: Colibri has no Burn, CubeCL, ONNX or ORT code path at all: a grep for onnxruntime|onnx|\bort\b|cubecl|\bburn\b over its C, headers, Makefiles, docs and Python returns six hits, every one the English word "burn" in a comment. There is nothing to run for this lane.
burn_cubecl_lane.not_wired_into_fennec: Deliberately not a dependency of the engine. Burn owns its allocator, so adopting it would mean giving up the three-tier residency that makes a 22.76 GiB int4 checkpoint run on a 31.5 GiB box at all. This lane is evidence about the framework, not a proposed backend swap.
